name: glulxe
why: A portable Glulx virtual machine running interactive fiction, a 32-bit cousin of the Z-machine with a quiet, old-school interpreter lineage worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Glulxe is the reference interpreter for Glulx, a portable virtual machine for interactive fiction. It takes a Glulx game file (usually compiled from Inform 6 source, often with a .ulx extension, or packaged in a Blorb .gblorb or .blb) and runs it, using a Glk library for input and output. It is a C program, and the homepage says it must be built against a Glk library. The Glulx VM itself is specified separately, currently at version 3.1.3, and the homepage also lists Quixe (a pure JavaScript Glulx interpreter for browsers) and Lectrote (Quixe packaged as a desktop app) as other ways to run the same games.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents Glulx as a 32-bit successor to the Z-machine. Per the homepage, it uses 32-bit data and addresses so game files can reach four gigabytes, and it has native Glk I/O so games can use any capability Glk provides, which the Z-machine lacks.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes Glulxe as a Glk program that executes Glulx bytecode, with the VM spec defining the opcodes, and it notes that Inform games are compiled to Glulx files by the standard Inform 6 compiler. The page does not explain interpreter internals beyond a note that memory-range checking is on by default since 0.5.0 and that a debugger module exists but is not compiled in by default.
brief.install_notes: The homepage does not give a build command. It says Glulxe is 'a Glk program, it must be built with a Glk library' and points to the Glk home page for that library. Source is offered as a 0.6.1 C tarball and a git repository, and ports are archived on the IF Archive. Brew installs the binary 'glulxe' per the formula metadata, so the Glk library question may be handled by the formula, but I did not verify that. The homepage also says Glulx games are played through the glulxe binary; no account or runtime is required.
brief.standout: Glulx is a 32-bit sibling of the Z-machine that the author treats as a documented, versioned spec with a public test suite of small games exercising each opcode and feature (glulxercise, unicodetest, memheaptest and others). The interpreter, spec, compiler and browser ports all sit on one site, with a 'Local Variable Mess' note on deprecating 8- and 16-bit locals, so the lineage is unusually visible.
brief.status: Quiet, not abandoned. The homepage says 'Last updated October 22, 2023'. Glulxe 0.6.1 is the current version named on the page, and the spec is at 3.1.3. The 'What's New' list is dated only by year (for example April 2020 for the Glk copyright transfer), and the author says he still acts as maintainer. I did not check the git repository or IF Archive dates.
brief.caveats: The homepage notes that 'The Glulxe version is slower' than the Z-code interpreter on the author's old 68040 hardware, though it is fine on a newer machine. The build requires a Glk library, which the page does not explain beyond a link. Several sample games are marked as needing specific older interpreter versions, such as Sensory Jam needing Glulxe 0.3.3, so not every game may run on the latest release without checking. I fetched only the homepage and did not read the git README or the Glk documentation, so build details are not verified.
quotes: Glulx is a portable VM, like the Z-machine. Unlike the Z-machine, it uses 32-bit data and addresses, so it can handle game files up to four gigabytes long.
Glulxe (for 'Glulx Execute') is the Glulx interpreter. The current version is 0.6.1.
The Glulxe version is slower. This is noticeable and annoying on my old (20MHz?) 68040 machine.
fetch_log: https://www.eblong.com/zarf/glulx/ : fetched OK, plain-text homepage with links to the spec, Glulxe, Quixe, Lectrote and sample games; the link URLs were not returned as text, so only the homepage is listed as a link.

judge.reason: Glulxe opens a window into Glulx, a documented 32-bit virtual machine built for interactive fiction, with its own bytecode, I/O model, and test games.

entry.title: glulxe
entry.tldr: The reference interpreter for Glulx, a 32-bit virtual machine for interactive fiction games, and a way to run text adventures built on a documented spec.
entry.deeper_look:
Glulxe ("Glulx Execute") runs Glulx game files. These are usually compiled from Inform 6 source and end in .ulx, or come packaged as Blorb files (.gblorb or .blb). It is a C program that does its input and output through a Glk library.

Glulx was designed as a successor to the Z-machine, the older virtual machine behind Infocom-era text adventures. In the author's words: "Glulx is a portable VM, like the Z-machine. Unlike the Z-machine, it uses 32-bit data and addresses, so it can handle game files up to four gigabytes long." It also has native Glk I/O, so games can use any capability Glk offers, which the Z-machine cannot.

The idea underneath is that a game is bytecode for a small, specified machine, so one file can run on any platform that has an interpreter. The Glulx spec is versioned (currently 3.1.3) and has a public test suite of small games that exercise individual opcodes and features. The interpreter, spec, compiler notes and browser ports are all documented on one site, so you can follow the whole lineage from source to running game. The same games also run in Quixe, a JavaScript interpreter for browsers, and in Lectrote, which packages Quixe as a desktop app.
entry.install:
brew install glulxe
# You need a Glulx game file (.ulx, .gblorb or .blb) to play. The homepage says Glulxe must be built against a Glk library; whether the formula handles that was not verified.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the interpreter's usage and options, which is the safest first look at what it accepts.

entry.whats_unique: Glulx is treated as a documented, versioned spec with a public test suite, and the interpreter, spec and browser ports sit side by side, so the lineage is unusually easy to follow.
entry.caveats: The homepage does not give build steps and says a Glk library is required, and some sample games need specific older Glulxe versions, so not every game is guaranteed to run on 0.6.1.
